name: Greeks
summary: The descendants of Javan, son of Japheth, whose culture spread across the East after Alexander the Great. Greek became the common language of the Roman world, the Old Testament was translated into it, and the whole New Testament was written in it. In Paul's letters 'Jew and Greek' together stand for all humanity, one in Christ.
name_meaning: Javan = Ionia (Greek Iaones), the Greeks of the Aegean coast. 'Greek' comes from Latin Graecus. The Greeks called themselves Hellenes.

origin.account: Javan was the fourth son of Japheth; his sons Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim peopled 'the isles of the Gentiles' — the Aegean islands, Cyprus (Kittim) and the Mediterranean coasts. Historically, Greek-speaking peoples are attested from the Mycenaean age (c. 1600–1100 BC, Linear B tablets), and classical Greek city-states flourished from the 8th century BC.

lineage.notes: Noah's blessing — 'God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem' — was read by early Christian writers as fulfilled when Greek-speaking Gentiles entered the church.

homeland.region: Greece, the Aegean islands and western Asia Minor ('the isles')
homeland.description: Mountainous peninsulas and islands of the Aegean, with colonies across the Mediterranean and Black Sea. After Alexander (336–323 BC), Greek cities and culture spread through Egypt, Syria, Judea and Mesopotamia — the Hellenistic world of the Ptolemies and Seleucids.
homeland.modern_location: Greece, Cyprus and western Turkey; historically Greek-speaking cities across the eastern Mediterranean.

places.name: Athens
places.note: Paul preached on Mars' hill about 'the unknown god'.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: Paul stayed eighteen months; two letters to its church.

places.name: Philippi
places.note: First church in Europe (Lydia, the jailer).

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Ionian Greek city where Paul taught two years.

places.name: Chittim (Kittim)
places.note: Named after a son of Javan.

timeline.event: Joel condemns Tyre and Sidon for selling Judeans 'unto the Grecians'.
Daniel's visions of the 'king of Grecia' — the he-goat with a notable horn, broken at its height and divided in four.
Alexander the Great conquers Persia, Egypt and the East; after his death his empire splits among his generals.
The Hebrew Scriptures are translated into Greek at Alexandria (the Septuagint).
The Seleucid Greek king Antiochus IV desecrates the Temple; the Maccabean revolt follows (Hanukkah). Many see this in Daniel's 'abomination that maketh desolate'.
Greeks at the Passover ask Philip, 'Sir, we would see Jesus'.
Complaints of the Grecians (Greek-speaking Jewish believers) lead to the appointment of the Seven.
At Antioch, believers first preach the Lord Jesus to Greeks, and the disciples are first called Christians.
Paul's missionary journeys plant churches across Macedonia, Achaia and Asia; Timothy and Titus, of Greek fathers, become his co-workers.

religion.practices: Civic polytheism, mystery cults and philosophy (Epicureans and Stoics). At Lystra the crowd called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercurius. At Ephesus the silversmiths rioted for Diana. Paul told the Athenians God 'hath made of one blood all nations of men' and now commands all to repent.

importance: The Greek world was the setting God used to spread the gospel. The New Testament was written in Koine Greek, and its authors quote the Septuagint. Greek audiences, who 'seek after wisdom', met Christ crucified, 'unto the Greeks foolishness', and many believed. Paul's gospel is 'to the Jew first, and also to the Greek', and in Christ 'there is neither Jew nor Greek'.

impact.how: Read the Scriptures in Greek; Greek-speaking synagogues were the first stops on Paul's journeys.
Greek-speaking widows' needs produced the first deacons, including Stephen.
Paul's closest helpers were part Greek or fully Greek.
The Jerusalem council decided Greeks need not be circumcised to be saved.

key_verses.text: And the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.
And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast: The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus.
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.

For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.

fate.summary: Greece came under Rome in 146 BC, but Greek remained the language of the eastern empire and of the early church. The Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire lasted until 1453, and modern Greece became independent in the 1820s–1830s.

today.summary: Modern Greeks (about 10 million in Greece, 0.7 million in Cyprus, plus a large diaspora) are the continuation of the ancient Greek-speaking world. The Greek Orthodox Church still reads the New Testament in its original Koine Greek.
today.modern_legacy: The Septuagint and the Greek New Testament. Words such as 'Bible', 'gospel' (evangelion), 'church' (ekklesia), 'baptism' and 'Christ' come from Greek.

archaeology.name: Gallio inscription (Delphi inscription)
archaeology.significance: Dates Gallio's proconsulship of Achaia, fixing the date of Paul's stay in Corinth.

archaeology.name: Erastus inscription
archaeology.significance: Names an Erastus who paved the square — possibly 'Erastus the chamberlain of the city'.

archaeology.name: Politarch inscriptions of Thessalonica
archaeology.significance: Confirm Luke's unusual title 'rulers of the city' (politarchs).
